content: Leanne Jones and Myfanwy Williams are members of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group based at the University of Liverpool in the United Kingdom. Theresa Lawrie serves as the Director of The Evidence-Based Medicine Consultancy Ltd, located in Bath, United Kingdom. Rodolfo Gomez Ponce de Leon is a Reproductive Health Advisor at the Latin American Center for Perinatology, Women, and Reproductive Health (CLAP/WR) in Montevideo, Uruguay. Tamar Kabakian is an Associate Professor specializing in Health Promotion and Community Health at the Faculty of Health Sciences, American University of Beirut, Lebanon. Petr Velebil is an obstetrician affiliated with the Perinatal Centre of the Institute for the Care of Mother and Child in Prague, Czech Republic. Yacouba Yaro is the Director General of the Center for Studies, Research, and Training for Economic and Social Development (CERFODES) in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso. Dr. Niveen Abu-Rmeileh, an expert in community and public health as well as statistical epidemiology, declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Luz Maria De-Regil, with expertise in nutrition, epidemiology, systematic reviews, and program implementation, disclosed authorship of publications on multiple micronutrient supplementation and vitamin D supplementation for pregnant women. She was previously employed by Nutrition International, a not-for-profit organization delivering micronutrient interventions, but this was not deemed a significant conflict of interest. Dr. Atf Ghérissi, specializing in systematic reviews, qualitative evidence, maternal and perinatal health, and community health, declared no conflicts of interest. Ms. Gill Gyte, a consumer representative in pregnancy and childbirth, declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Rintaro Mori, an expert in perinatology, neonatology, systematic reviews, evidence synthesis, and guideline development using GRADE, also declared no conflicts of interest. Prof. Jim Neilson, specializing in general obstetrics, perinatology, gynecology, systematic reviews, and evidence synthesis, declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Lynnette Neufeld, an expert in micronutrients, programs, and epidemiology, declared no conflicts of interest, and her participation in technical consultations was unaffected. Prof. Nafissa Osman, specializing in obstetrics, gynecology, and implementation research, declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Erika Ota, with expertise in nutrition, evidence synthesis, and guideline development, also declared no conflicts of interest. Prof. Robert Pattinson, an expert in obstetrics, gynecology, care delivery, and evidence synthesis, declared no conflicts of interest. Prof. Harshi Sachdev contributed data from India to meta-analyses and co-authored a paper on multiple micronutrients in pregnancy, but this was not considered a significant conflict of interest. Ms. Rusidah Selamat, specializing in maternal and infant nutrition, community-based programs, and implementation research, declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Charlotte Warren, an expert in maternal and perinatal health, systematic reviews, and implementation research, declared no conflicts of interest. Prof. Charles Wiysonge, specializing in health systems, systematic reviews, and care delivery, also declared no conflicts of interest. Regarding antenatal vitamin D supplementation, studies compared the effects of vitamin D alone versus placebo or no intervention during pregnancy. These studies were conducted in various countries, including Australia, Bangladesh, Brazil, China, France, India, Iran, New Zealand, Pakistan, Russia, and the United Kingdom. However, most outcome data were derived from studies in India and Iran. The findings were based on a Cochrane systematic review by Palacios et al. (2019), which was also used in the revised 2019 WHO meta-analysis.g., women at risk of eclampsia or gestational diabetes). Wide confidence intervals and limited events further contributed to the low certainty of the evidence. Similarly, the effects of combined vitamin D and calcium supplementation versus no supplementation were evaluated, with most data derived from studies in India and Iran. The evidence was again rated as very low quality due to imprecision, few events, and potential bias in the included studies.
